results.note: Methods › Information sources and search strategy: nine databases and registries (Medline, CINAHL, PsycInfo, Embase, CENTRAL, ICTRP, ClinicalTrials.gov, Web of Science, Scopus) from inception to 25 March 2026, no date or language limits. Results › Amphetamine-induced psychosis studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs: eight RCTs with 514 participants (the Table 1 sizes sum to 514), two placebo-controlled, five of 25–28 days and the others 6, 8 and 12 weeks. Table 1: Sulaiman 2013 aripiprazole 19 vs placebo 18, outpatient, 8 weeks; Wang 2019 paliperidone 40 vs placebo 40, 84 days ('extended-release' is in the reference-list title of Wang et al. 2019, not in Table 1). Table 2 note and Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs: no study of relapse after antipsychotics were stopped, so the optimal duration could not be addressed; the 5th paragraph also says the studies were unsuitable for meta-analysis. The six head-to-head trials in Table 1 are those of card sc_srisurapanont_2021. Role supports: right.

Methods › Measures of effect: d = (baseline mean − end-point mean) / pooled SD. Table 2: every arm of the five 4-week trials d 3.402 to 5.495; between-group p 0.06 (Wang 2020), 0.32 (Verachai), 0.73 (Wang 2016), ns (Samiei), 0.07 (Leelahanaj); Sulaiman 2013 between-group 0.032 with footnote c (MMRM); Wang 2019 PANSS 37.8 (5.4) to 34 (3.9) and 36.2 (4.3) to 32.9 (1.9), between-group 0.006 with footnote d (Cox regression). Primary outcomes › Amphetamine-induced psychosis, 4th paragraph: stabilised in voluntary drug-treatment wards before discharge. Table 3, 2a-2: lost to follow-up 11 (28%) vs 22 (55%), OR 0.31 (0.12, 0.79). Editors' checks recomputed: Samiei 45.7 / (14.4/√2) = 4.488 and 47.4 / (12.2/√2) = 5.495, i.e. an end-point SD of zero; falls of 3.8 and 3.3 points. Role qualifies: right.

ClinicalTrials.gov Record History, read version by version. Outcome Measures changed only in versions 2 (2018-03-30), 14 and 15. Versions 7 (2019-04-26), 12 (2023-07-02) and 13 (2025-07-04): primary outcome 'relative risk of psychosis relapse', time frame 36 months; transition to schizophrenia (DSM-5) at 36 months. Version 14 (2025-11-12): primary BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months. Version 15 (2026-03-23, current): primary CGI-S, CGI-I and CGI-E at 12 and 24 months, BPRS-24 secondary. Primary completion 2024-05-31 [Actual] from version 13. Current eligibility excludes people who 'had been diagnosed to have Schizophrenia' (schizoaffective disorder is not named). On whether follow-up was cut from 36 to 24 months before the outcome change: no. The registry never recorded a 24-month design before then; every 36-month time frame became 24 months in the same version 14, after actual primary completion (31 May 2024) and actual study completion (31 May 2025). Version 12 still gave 36 months, status 'Recruiting' and estimated primary completion 2024-05-31. The registry's actual study completion (31 May 2025) is a year after the article's final follow-up (31 May 2024). Role qualifies: right.

results.note: Table 1: Kittirattanapaiboon (2010), Thailand, 39%, 1116 people, 5.0 years, 40% followed up, hospital, file review; reference 13's title describes long-term outcomes of methamphetamine psychosis after a first hospitalisation. Medhus (2016 in Table 1; reference 72 dated 2015, a 'small prospective sample' with amphetamine-induced psychosis): 33%, 29 people, 6.0 years, 41%. Niemi-Pynttäri (2013), Finland: 6%, 18 478 (reference 16: all substance-induced inpatient cases). No substance-specific figures are shown for single studies. The comparison with the 2019 systematic review is an editors' comparison (card sc_voce_2019) and cannot be checked here. An addition worth considering (editors' calculation): Table 3's 'Other' diagnostic-system subgroup (2 studies, 459 subjects) holds only this cohort and Wright (1988, 10 people), so the Thai cohort entered the analyses with about 449 people (40.2% of 1116, its followed-up share), not 1116. Role qualifies: right.

All numbers match (Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, 2nd paragraph; Subgroup Analysis; Tables 3 and 4; Limitations, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). Correction of wording only. The review states its P < .01 threshold for the categorical subgroup analyses, not for the meta-regressions, and its abstract and discussion report the age association as a finding (transition slightly lower in older cohorts), so 'no study feature predicted transition' overstates the null for age. The quotation is verbatim (Methods, 1st paragraph; 11 words). Role qualifies: right.
results.corrected_extracted: The five amphetamine estimates are not identified in the article, and the methods record methamphetamine, amphetamine and cocaine psychoses together as stimulant-induced. No categorical study feature predicted transition at the review's Bonferroni threshold for subgroup comparisons (P < .01). In meta-regression, for which no threshold is stated, length of follow-up (P = .3433) and percentage followed up (β −1.716, P = .0785; lower transition with more complete follow-up) were not associated. Older cohorts had lower transition (β −0.050, P = .0286), which the review reports as a finding and suggests may be ecological. Few studies recorded the amount of use before the episode, comorbid substance use disorders or continued use; most diagnoses came from registers or routine care (research interviews in 8 studies, 127 people). The authors state that substance-induced is used by convention, not as a presumed causal link.
